opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the balance of power right now is deeply lopsided, and that's really what motivated a lot of our work. On one side you have some of the best-resourced companies in the world, with enormous compute budgets, armies of lawyers, and the ability to scrape essentially anything that's been posted publicly online. On the other side you have individual artists, illustrators, photographers, many of whom are freelancers working paycheck to paycheck, who have no real visibility into whether their work has been taken, and very little practical recourse if it has.

The mechanisms that are supposed to protect them just haven't kept up. Opt-out lists and do-not-crawl directives are entirely voluntary, and there's no way to verify they're being honored. Litigation takes years and is expensive, and the outcome is uncertain. And regulation is moving, but slowly, and unevenly across different countries. So in the meantime, the default is basically: your work gets used unless you can somehow prove otherwise and fight it, which is a burden most artists simply can't carry.

What we've seen talking with thousands of artists is that this isn't abstract for them. People are losing commissions, losing jobs, seeing models fine-tuned specifically to mimic their personal style, sometimes with their name attached as a prompt. And there's a real emotional toll, too. A lot of young artists are asking themselves whether it's even worth pursuing this as a career.

So the way I think about tools like Glaze and Nightshade is that they're an attempt to give artists some leverage back. Glaze is about protecting an individual's style from mimicry. Nightshade is more about changing the economics: if scraping without consent carries some risk of degrading your model, then licensing and actually asking permission starts to look like the more attractive path. We're not trying to stop AI research or say generative models shouldn't exist. The goal is to shift things so that consent and compensation become the norm rather than the exception.

I'll be honest that technical tools alone won't fix this. You need legal and policy changes, and you need norms within the industry to evolve. But technology can buy time, and it can give people who otherwise have zero power at least something they can do today, on their own terms.

r001.rationale: It says opt-out lists are entirely voluntary and there is no way to verify companies honor them.

r002.rationale: It says artists lack visibility into whether their work was used, but does not state that models cannot definitively determine whether a particular image was in training.

r003.rationale: It favors consent and compensation and says licensing should become more attractive, but does not advocate requiring companies to train on licensed data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the short answer is that it's wildly asymmetric, and that's really what got us into this space in the first place. You have on one side companies with billions of dollars in compute, legal teams, and the ability to scrape basically the entire public internet in a matter of weeks. And on the other side you have individual artists, illustrators, concept artists, people who are often freelancers, who have essentially no leverage. They can't opt out in any meaningful way, because opt-out mechanisms, where they exist, are voluntary, they're inconsistent, and frankly a lot of the scraping already happened before anyone was asking.

What struck me when we started talking to artists a few years ago was that the harm wasn't abstract. People were seeing their names used as style prompts. They were seeing clients come back and say, "we don't need the commission anymore, we generated something in your style." So the training data isn't just being used to build a general-purpose model, it's being used to directly compete with the very people it was taken from. That's a pretty unusual dynamic economically.

And the legal system is slow. Copyright law was not written with this in mind, and these cases are going to take years to resolve. Meanwhile the technology moves on monthly. So artists are being told, essentially, "wait and see," while the facts on the ground get decided for them.

That's really the gap that tools like Glaze and Nightshade are trying to fill. The idea isn't that a piece of software is going to fix a structural power imbalance. It's not. The idea is to give artists some agency right now, some technical means to say "no" that doesn't depend on a company's goodwill or a court ruling that may be five years away. If scraping has a cost, if there's at least some friction, then suddenly licensing and consent start to look like reasonable business decisions rather than something you do out of charity.

So I'd say the balance of power is still very much tilted toward the AI companies. But I'm somewhat encouraged that the conversation has shifted. Two or three years ago the default assumption was that anything on the public internet is fair game, full stop. Now at least there's a real debate, there are licensing deals happening, and there's recognition that creators have a stake in this. Whether that turns into durable protections is still an open question, and I think it depends a lot on whether artists, and the public more broadly, keep pushing.

r001.rationale: The response says opt-out mechanisms, where they exist, are voluntary and inconsistent, indicating they depend on companies choosing to honor them.

r002.rationale: The response does not address whether current models can determine if a particular image was used in training.

r003.rationale: The response discusses licensing and consent, but does not advocate requiring AI companies to train on licensed data.

astra-6.text:
I think the balance is heavily tilted toward the AI companies. They have the compute, the capital, and the ability to collect work at a scale that individual artists can’t really contest. An artist can say, “I don’t want my work used this way,” but that means very little if there’s no practical way to enforce that choice.

To me, the central issue is consent. Sharing your art so people can see it shouldn’t automatically mean giving a company permission to train a commercial model on it. Artists should have a meaningful say in whether their work is used and under what terms.

Getting there requires more than asking companies to behave responsibly. It requires ways for artists to exercise that choice, and rules that give that choice some force. Otherwise, one side gets to set the terms, and the other side is left reacting.

r003.rationale: The response calls for meaningful artist choice and enforceable rules, but does not advocate requiring companies to train on licensed data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the balance of power is heavily tilted toward the AI companies. They have the computing resources, the money, and the ability to collect work at enormous scale. An individual artist has very little ability to even find out whether their work was used, much less negotiate the terms of that use.

And that’s really the central issue: who gets to make that decision? Sharing your work online shouldn’t mean giving up any say in how it’s used. Artists should have a meaningful opportunity to consent, to say no, and to negotiate compensation if they choose to participate.

Getting there takes more than asking companies to behave better. You need enforceable rules, collective bargaining power, and technical tools that give artists some practical control. Otherwise, the people building these systems get to set the terms, and the people whose work makes those systems valuable are left reacting.
